definition: Stabilize means to make something steady and keep it from getting worse.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word stabilize. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know stabilize should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A snack every three hours stabilizes her blood sugar through the long double shifts.
Steadying is the moment's fix — a hand on the wobbling ladder — and it stops short of stabilizing, which builds the steadiness in so it holds after you let go.
Cement goes further than stabilize — a stabilized arrangement holds and stops slipping, while a cemented one is fixed for good and may never move again.

To secure something is to fasten it so it cannot move or be taken — locks, knots, bolts, a boat tied fast to the dock. Stabilizing fights a different enemy: decline. Something failing gets made steady so it stops getting worse. You secure a sound thing in place; you stabilize a failing one.

To anchor is to fix something firmly in one place, usually with sheer weight — a tent staked down, a bookcase bolted to the wall. Stabilizing is about condition rather than location: a failing patient, market, or porch stops getting worse. Anchoring holds a position; to stabilize is to halt a decline.

To brace something is to add support before the blow — you brace a shelf for heavy books or yourself for impact. Stabilizing answers a different problem: something already wobbling or worsening gets made steady so it stops sliding further. Bracing prepares for trouble; to stabilize is to arrest trouble already underway.

Stabilize means to make something steady and keep it from getting worse.

The park district's old carousel had begun to lean and shed bolts, so the first hire was not a painter but a millwright to stabilize it: new footings under the center pole, fresh bracing in the frame, a governor to cap its speed.
The horses stayed shabby for another season, but the ride stopped getting worse — which bought the restoration fund time.
Stabilize is the precise verb because the goal is not improvement but arrest: make the thing steady and keep it from sliding further.
Repair would overstate what the millwright did — the shabbiness remains.
First you stabilize; then, when money allows, you restore.
Stabilize is the triage verb: it promises steadiness, not improvement — the patient, the currency, or the leaning porch stops getting worse, and better comes later, if at all.
Its unit-mates divide the work: buttress adds strength, withstand endures the blow, and robust describes what needs no help.
For a quick physical fix, steady is the plainer verb.

The helicopter crew's first job was never to cure anything, the flight nurse explained -- it was to keep the patient from getting worse.
A climber comes off the ridge with internal bleeding, and the protocols exist to stabilize him: fluids in, pressure held, vitals watched every minute.
Nothing done in the cabin fixes the injury; the surgery that will do that waits ninety miles away.
Success, on this leg of the trip, is written in numbers that stop falling -- blood pressure holding, pulse steady, nothing sliding further.
The nurse put it simply: the mountain does the harm, the hospital does the healing, and the helicopter's whole art is holding the line between them.
